comments.note: MysqlDumpBackupService.cs line 81: `await using var outputFile = new FileStream(...)` does not apply .ConfigureAwait(false) to the DisposeAsync call. FileStream implements IAsyncDisposable, so the disposal is technically an unconfigured await. Could be written as `await using (new FileStream(...).ConfigureAwait(false))`. Risk is negligible in an Infrastructure service with no captured sync context, but worth addressing for strict AC6 compliance.

MysqlDumpBackupServiceTests: no explicit test for connection values containing shell metacharacters (spaces, quotes, semicolons, pipe). While the ArgumentList mechanism makes injection impossible by design, a test would document the invariant and prevent future regressions if the implementation were ever changed to use Arguments string form.

BackupAsync: if destinationFolder does not exist, FileStream creation throws DirectoryNotFoundException. This is caught and returned as a failure result (safe), but a Directory.CreateDirectory(destinationFolder) guard before the FileStream open would give callers a better experience. Alternatively, document that the caller must ensure the folder exists.

summary: Reviewed 3 files: MysqlDumpBackupService.cs, Program.cs, MysqlDumpBackupServiceTests.cs. 0 Critical, 0 High, 1 Medium, 2 Low findings. Security sign-off: PASS. The core injection-prevention design (ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList with UseShellExecute=false) is correct and eliminates shell command injection entirely. The main residual concern is the database password being transiently visible in OS process listings (-p flag), which is a known mysqldump limitation and is Medium severity given the desktop-only threat model.

comments.note: Medium — A02/A07 (Cryptographic Failures / Identification & Authentication Failures): MysqlDumpBackupService.cs line 150 — password passed as '-p{conn.Password}' in ArgumentList. While ArgumentList prevents shell injection, the password is transiently visible in OS process command-line listings (Task Manager Details column on Windows; /proc/{pid}/cmdline and `ps aux` on Linux/macOS) for the duration of the mysqldump process. Any local user or monitoring tool with process inspection rights can read it. Remediation: write a temporary '--defaults-extra-file' file containing '[client]\npassword=...' with restrictive permissions (owner-read-only), pass '--defaults-extra-file=<path>' as an ArgumentList entry instead, and delete the temp file in a finally block after WaitForExitAsync returns.

Low — A01 (Broken Access Control / Path Traversal): MysqlDumpBackupService.cs line 64 — outputFileName is built by concatenating conn.Database with a timestamp: `$"{databaseName}_{timestamp}.sql"`. If conn.Database contains path-separator characters (e.g. `../`, `..\\`), Path.Combine(destinationFolder, outputFileName) can resolve to a path outside the intended destination folder, silently writing the dump to an unexpected location. Although conn.Database comes from the user's own settings store (not external input), this is still poor hygiene. Remediation: sanitize databaseName before use in a filename — replace or remove any characters that are invalid in file names: `var safeName = string.Concat(databaseName.Split(Path.GetInvalidFileNameChars()))` or use a regex to strip `[/\\:*?"<>|]`.

Low — A04 (Insecure Design): MysqlDumpBackupService.cs lines 81-97 — if the CancellationToken fires after the FileStream is opened but before WaitForExitAsync completes, the catch block does not match OperationCanceledException (it is rethrown), and the partially-written .sql file at outputFilePath is left on disk. Consumers may mistake a truncated dump for a valid backup. Remediation: in the catch/finally block, attempt File.Delete(outputFilePath) when ex is OperationCanceledException or when the file size is 0 bytes, to avoid leaving a corrupt partial backup.

Info — A09 (Security Logging): MysqlDumpBackupService.cs line 107 — on non-zero exit, the full mysqldump stderr is logged at LogError level. Stderr routinely includes 'Warning: Using a password on the command line interface can be insecure.' MySQL may in future include more context in stderr. The current log does not expose the password itself, so this is informational only. No action required.

summary: Reviewed MysqlDumpBackupService.cs, Program.cs, and MysqlDumpBackupServiceTests.cs line-by-line.
Architecture is clean: interface in Core, implementation in Infrastructure, singleton registration in App. No cross-layer violations.
Injection-safety design is correct: ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList + UseShellExecute=false passes all field values directly to the OS API without shell expansion.
Error handling is correct: all failure paths return DatabaseBackupResult(false, null, msg). Non-cancellation exceptions are caught and returned. OperationCanceledException correctly propagates.

Process lifecycle on cancellation: the `using var process` ensures Process.Dispose() closes the stdout pipe after CancellationToken fires mid-CopyToAsync — mysqldump exits via broken-pipe. Implicit but safe.
BuildStartInfo dead outputFilePath parameter: unused inside the method body, explicitly documented in XML. Deliberate testability design — no change required.

All acceptance criteria verified: ArgumentList populated, Arguments string form never used, early-return on missing binary folder, stderr returned on non-zero exit, InternalsVisibleTo present, ConfigureAwait on all standard awaits, zero build warnings.
No blocking issues found. PASS.

comments.note: MysqlDumpBackupService.cs — BuildStartInfo: the `outputFilePath` parameter is never used inside the method body. The XML doc clearly explains this is intentional (testability hook). No change required; the comment is sufficient. Future consideration: if the implementation migrates to --result-file= instead of stdout streaming, this parameter becomes functional.

MysqlDumpBackupService.cs lines 81–97 — process lifecycle on cancellation: when CancellationToken fires mid-CopyToAsync, the `using var process` ensures Process.Dispose() is called synchronously as the async method unwinds, which closes the stdout redirect pipe and causes mysqldump to exit via broken-pipe (EPIPE/ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE). This is safe but implicit. Consider adding an explicit `process.Kill(entireProcessTree: true)` in a finally block or a try/catch on the OperationCanceledException re-throw to make the cleanup intent clear to future maintainers.

MysqlDumpBackupServiceTests.cs — no test asserts that ArgumentList contains the correct number of entries (10 arguments). The existing ContainInOrder test verifies order and content but would still pass if extra entries were appended. A `HaveCount(10)` assertion on psi.ArgumentList would lock down the full argument shape.

[documentation-forward] IDatabaseBackupService.cs — the class-level XML summary says 'by invoking the mysqldump utility', which leaks the concrete implementation detail into the interface definition. The interface should describe the operation abstractly (e.g., 'Performs a full database backup and writes the dump to a caller-supplied destination folder') without referencing mysqldump, so alternative implementations remain valid.

MysqlDumpBackupService.cs line 81 — `await using var outputFile = new FileStream(...)` does not configure the implicit DisposeAsync await. FileStream implements IAsyncDisposable so disposal is a ConfigureAwait(false)-eligible await. Risk is negligible in an Infrastructure service (no captured sync context), but noted for strict AC6 compliance. Already flagged by QA.
